item.title: When one more occupier means you need an HMO licence (and can be fined)
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Landlords renting out properties to multiple tenants need to be aware of the rules surrounding Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs). These properties, where three or more unrelated individuals share living spaces, come with specific licensing requirements. Understanding these regulations is crucial to avoid potential fines and legal complications.

What Defines an HMO?

An HMO is typically a property rented to three or more people who form more than one household. A household can include individuals, couples, or family members, and in some cases, live-in employees such as carers or nannies. In England, properties with five or more occupants from two or more households usually require an HMO licence from the local council. This licence specifies the maximum number of occupants and the property standards that must be met. Smaller HMOs may also need a licence if local authorities have additional licensing schemes in place.

The Importance of Licensing for Landlords

Many landlords aim to avoid licensing by limiting the number of occupants. However, this can be challenging as tenants may bring in friends or relatives to share the property, often without the landlord’s knowledge. For example, tenants might move in a partner or take on unauthorised lodgers to help with rent. Landlords must remain vigilant and conduct regular inspections to ensure occupancy limits are not exceeded. Failing to do so could lead to unintentional breaches of housing laws.

Under section 72(1) of the Housing Act 2004, landlords who manage or control an unlicensed HMO that requires a licence may be committing a housing offence. This applies even if the breach occurs unknowingly. For instance, in a case involving Derby City Council, landlord Mr Sejmir Mehmeti faced legal action after temporarily exceeding the occupancy limit at his property. Although he had previously adhered to the rules, a short period of over-occupation led to penalties, highlighting the importance of strict compliance.

Key Takeaways for Landlords

  • Regularly inspect properties to ensure occupancy limits are not exceeded.
  • Be aware of local licensing schemes, which may apply even to smaller HMOs.
  • Communicate clearly with tenants about the rules regarding additional occupants.
  • Understand that unintentional breaches can still result in legal consequences.

Navigating HMO regulations can be complex, but staying informed and proactive can help landlords avoid costly mistakes. By adhering to licensing requirements and maintaining open communication with tenants, property owners can ensure compliance and protect their investments.

item.title: Should tenants pay to restore an overgrown garden at the end of a tenancy?
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Disputes over garden maintenance are a frequent point of contention between landlords and tenants at the end of a tenancy. A recent case highlights the importance of clear documentation and understanding responsibilities when it comes to garden upkeep. The landlord claimed that the tenant had returned the property with an overgrown garden, necessitating professional gardening services to restore it before new tenants moved in. The tenant, however, argued that the garden had been maintained during their stay. This disagreement underscores the need for both parties to be aware of their obligations and to keep thorough records.

The Importance of Check-In and Check-Out Reports

In this case, the landlord relied on the check-in inventory, which described the garden as well-maintained, with neatly cut grass, trimmed shrubs, and weed-free borders. Photographs taken at the start of the tenancy supported this description. The check-out report, however, recorded long grass, substantial weed growth, and overgrown planting areas. These reports, alongside photographic evidence, played a crucial role in the adjudicator’s decision. Landlords and tenants alike may benefit from ensuring that check-in and check-out reports are thorough and accurately reflect the condition of the garden.

Understanding Tenancy Agreements

Tenancy agreements often include clauses about garden maintenance, specifying whether the tenant is responsible for routine upkeep. In this instance, the adjudicator reviewed the tenancy agreement and determined that the tenant had a responsibility to maintain the garden to the standard recorded at check-in. Homeowners may wish to ensure that tenancy agreements clearly outline these responsibilities to avoid misunderstandings. Similarly, tenants might consider reviewing their agreements to understand their obligations before moving in.

Ultimately, the adjudicator awarded the landlord compensation for the costs incurred in restoring the garden. This case serves as a reminder of the importance of clear documentation and understanding responsibilities when it comes to garden maintenance in rental properties.

item.title: Landlords seek 10% rent rises but tribunals award just 6.2%
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

New research reveals a significant gap between the rent increases landlords request and what tribunals actually approve in England. Analysis of 336 tribunal decisions shows landlords typically seek 10% hikes but secure just 6.2% on average, with nearly one in ten cases failing before reaching the assessment stage.

The Rent Rise Reality Gap

Lettings firm Hello Neighbour examined tribunal outcomes following changes under the Renters’ Rights Act. Their findings demonstrate that whilst 237 of 300 assessed cases resulted in rent increases, only 105 landlords obtained their full requested amount. In contrast, 43 cases saw no change, and 20 tenants actually paid less after tribunal rulings.

Regional variations paint an interesting picture. Northern landlords fared worst, with median requests of 15.4% reduced to 9.4% awards. Southern areas (excluding London) saw requested 8% increases typically cut to just 3%. London landlords experienced a smaller gap, with 8.1% requests commonly adjusted to 5.6% approvals.

Why Landlord Applications Fail

Approximately one in eleven cases collapsed due to procedural errors before rent assessments began. London proved particularly problematic, accounting for 20 of the 32 failed applications - roughly one in seven capital cases failing versus one in twenty elsewhere.

Common mistakes included:

  • Setting new rent start dates mid-tenancy period
  • Using outdated Form 4 instead of current Form 4A
  • Providing insufficient notice periods
  • Failing to include all joint tenants
  • Unauthorised email notices without tenant agreement

Even minor administrative errors proved costly - one Newham landlord lost their case by breaching the 52-week rule by just 24 hours.

The Evidence Challenge

Weak supporting evidence frequently undermined landlord cases. Tribunals only directly considered named comparable properties in 73 of 300 decisions, whilst 53 cases proceeded with no usable evidence at all.

Many landlords relied on portal asking prices (submitted in 247 cases) rather than achieved rents (presented in just 139 instances). Common evidential shortcomings included missing property addresses, absent transaction dates, omitted floor areas (in 70% of cases), and inappropriate comparisons between different property types or sizes.

For landlords considering rent increases, these findings highlight the importance of thorough preparation, accurate paperwork and robust comparable evidence - particularly where tenants might challenge proposed hikes.

item.title: Goodlord launches new tools as letting agents grapple with Renters’ Rights Act
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Lettings technology provider Goodlord has unveiled a suite of new tools designed to help agents navigate the challenges posed by the Renters’ Rights Act. The updates include comparable rent reports, tribunal decision tracking and streamlined insurance claims processing, alongside new integrations with property software platforms.

Enhanced tools for rent reviews and tribunal insights

From November, Goodlord will automatically generate Comparable Rent Reports when landlords conduct rent reviews through its platform. These reports analyse rental prices for similar properties in the local area, providing agents with data to support proposed increases. This development comes as the Renters’ Rights Act brings greater scrutiny to rent adjustments.

Alongside this, the company has launched a publicly accessible database tracking First-tier Tribunal decisions on rental disputes. The regularly updated resource allows agents to monitor local rulings and identify trends in how tribunals are interpreting the new legislation. Such insights could prove valuable when advising landlords on rent adjustments or dispute resolution.

Streamlined insurance claims and new partnerships

Goodlord has introduced a dedicated claims dashboard for agents managing rent protection insurance. The system incorporates AI to help compile documentation and promises quicker processing times, with the company reporting that 92% of cases now receive a response within two working days. Their insurance partner reportedly settles 88% of claims within one working day.

The company has also expanded its ecosystem through two strategic partnerships. A new integration with Hammock provides landlords with accounting software access through Goodlord’s Landlord Hub, helping them prepare for Making Tax Digital requirements. Additionally, an expanded relationship with Reapit aims to enhance workflow connectivity between platforms.

Industry challenges post-legislation

These innovations follow Goodlord’s recent industry research, which revealed that 46% of letting agents find tenancy management has become less predictable since the Renters’ Rights Act came into force. The study, surveying over 3,000 industry participants, also found 27% of landlords have either reduced their portfolios or are considering doing so.

For letting agents adapting to the post-Renters’ Rights Act landscape, these new tools might offer valuable support in maintaining compliance while efficiently managing landlord and tenant relationships. As the rental market continues to evolve, such technological solutions could play an increasingly important role in property administration.

item.title: Rents set to rise twice as fast as house prices – Hamptons
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Rental prices across Great Britain are predicted to climb at double the rate of house prices over the next three years, according to recent analysis by Hamptons. The estate agency forecasts that rents on newly agreed tenancies will surge by 14.2% between 2026 and 2029, compared to a more modest 7.2% rise in house prices during the same period. This widening gap highlights the growing pressures within the rental market, driven by shrinking supply and increasing demand.

Supply Shortages and Rising Demand

The rental market is facing a significant imbalance, with the number of available properties in October 2023 down by 26% compared to a decade ago. In London, the situation is even more acute, with a 39% decline in rental homes. Meanwhile, tenant demand continues to grow, with 10% more people searching for rental properties than a year earlier. This mismatch between supply and demand is expected to intensify competition among renters, pushing prices upwards despite affordability challenges.

Landlords Retreat Amid Rising Costs

Higher costs for landlords, including increased taxes and mortgage rates, alongside stricter regulations under the Renters’ Rights Act, are discouraging investment in the buy-to-let sector. Hamptons reports that landlords accounted for just 10.1% of property purchases in 2023—the lowest proportion since the agency began tracking this data in 2010. While some regions, such as the North East, remain relatively strong for investor activity, purchases are failing to offset the number of landlords exiting the market. This trend is contributing to the ongoing reduction in rental supply.

Tax Changes Add Pressure

Tax reforms introduced over the past decade have significantly increased the financial burden on landlords. Hamptons estimates that these changes will generate an additional £4.3bn annually for the Treasury, equating to around £900 per tenancy in England each year. From April 2027, a further four-percentage-point increase in landlord income tax rates is expected to raise an additional £950m annually. These rising costs, combined with higher mortgage rates and regulatory demands, are making buy-to-let investments increasingly difficult to sustain.

Whilst some landlords continue to invest, the overall decline in rental supply suggests that the market will remain under pressure for the foreseeable future. Renters may face higher costs and fiercer competition, whilst landlords navigate a challenging financial landscape. Homeowners and investors alike might consider seeking professional advice to understand how these trends could impact their financial plans.

item.title: Your letting agent deals with everything—but who checks the agent?
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Many landlords in England rely on letting agents to handle the day-to-day management of their rental properties. Whilst this can provide welcome peace of mind, homeowners may wish to remember that ultimate responsibility still lies with them. Even with professional management in place, landlords could face penalties if legal obligations aren't met—making periodic checks on your agent's work a sensible precaution.

Understanding your agency agreement

The foundation of the landlord-agent relationship is the agency agreement. This contract outlines exactly what services the letting agent provides, from tenant sourcing to full property management. Landlords might consider reviewing this document carefully to clarify:

  • Whether the service covers let-only, rent collection or full management
  • Which party handles safety checks, deposit protection and repairs
  • What requires explicit landlord approval before action
  • How frequently property inspections should occur
  • Protocols for reporting urgent maintenance issues

Without this understanding, landlords may unfairly criticise agents for services not included in their agreement. It could be worth keeping a copy of this document accessible and referring to it periodically to ensure all contracted services are being delivered.

Monitoring tenant selection and ongoing management

One of the primary reasons landlords use agents is for tenant sourcing and vetting. However, some landlords have discovered too late that their agent's referencing process wasn't as thorough as expected. Whilst agents typically handle tenant selection, landlords remain ultimately responsible for ensuring proper checks are conducted.

Borrowers might consider requesting copies of tenant referencing documents, though some agents may be reluctant to share these. Other areas to monitor include:

  • Confirming all legally required safety certificates are current and properly filed
  • Checking that tenant deposits are protected in a government-approved scheme
  • Verifying that rent payments are being processed correctly and on time
  • Ensuring maintenance issues are addressed promptly and properly documented

Whilst most letting agents provide excellent service, landlords may wish to remember that periodic oversight helps protect their investment and ensures compliance. A hands-off approach could lead to unpleasant surprises, particularly if local authorities investigate tenant complaints or when possession proceedings become necessary.

Establishing clear communication channels with your agent and scheduling regular updates could help landlords stay informed without micromanaging. Many find that striking this balance allows them to benefit from professional management whilst maintaining appropriate oversight of their property.

item.title: The Guild’s ‘Cornflakes and Compliance’ reaches 200 episodes
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The Guild of Property Professionals has recently celebrated a significant milestone with the release of the 200th episode of its popular weekly compliance series, Cornflakes and Compliance. This innovative video series has become a valuable resource for estate and letting agents, offering guidance on navigating the ever-changing landscape of property legislation and regulatory requirements.

Supporting Agents with Compliance Challenges

Hosted by Paul Offley, the Guild’s compliance officer, Cornflakes and Compliance delivers weekly updates on critical topics such as anti-money laundering (AML) obligations, proposed legislative changes, and compliance procedures. Each episode also provides a platform for Guild members to submit questions, ensuring that agents can seek clarity on issues they encounter in their daily operations. This interactive approach has made the series particularly effective in addressing the practical challenges faced by professionals in the property industry.

Offley explained that the series was designed to simplify complex regulatory requirements, making them more accessible for agents. “When we launched Cornflakes and Compliance, our goal was to offer straightforward, digestible guidance that members could easily absorb, perhaps whilst enjoying their morning coffee,” he said. He emphasised that compliance is a constantly evolving area, with new developments and questions arising regularly.

A Lifeline for Independent Agents

Iain McKenzie, Chief Executive of the Guild of Property Professionals, highlighted the challenges faced by independent agents in staying abreast of regulatory changes whilst managing their businesses. “For independent agencies, keeping up with legislation and compliance requirements can be particularly demanding,” he noted. “The weekly updates provided by Cornflakes and Compliance help members stay informed and better understand their responsibilities.”

The series is released every Wednesday, with previous episodes available on the Guild’s Members’ Hub and Learning Platform. This accessibility ensures that agents can revisit key topics and refresh their knowledge as needed.

The 200th episode arrives at a time when estate and letting agents are navigating a period of significant legislative change, alongside existing obligations such as AML and consumer protection. The Guild’s initiative underscores its commitment to supporting its members through these challenges, ensuring they remain compliant and well-informed.

As the property sector continues to evolve, resources like Cornflakes and Compliance play a crucial role in helping agents adapt to new requirements and maintain high standards of professionalism.

item.title: EYE NEWSFLASH: BestAgent breaks silence on viewing charges and property listings after bruising week
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

BestAgent has issued a detailed response to recent criticism surrounding its property listing policies and viewing charges, following a turbulent week for the online platform. The statement comes shortly after the resignation of Yopa CEO Verona Frankish from BestAgent's advisory board, amid reported concerns about the company's strategic direction.

Viewing Charge Controversy Explained

The dispute emerged after a Suffolk estate agent tested BestAgent's viewing system and received an £8 plus VAT payment request to confirm a property viewing appointment. BestAgent has since clarified that genuine buyer and tenant enquiries remain free, suggesting the charge may have appeared during system testing. The company maintains it has never intentionally charged agents for applicant enquiries, offering refunds for any accidental payments.

While defending its current free enquiry model, BestAgent acknowledged plans to introduce a pay-per-lead system in future. The proposed charges would vary according to property price points, which the company argues could give agents more control over marketing expenditure compared to traditional portal subscription models.

Property Listings and Advisory Changes

BestAgent's statement also addressed concerns about its approach to property listings, reaffirming its position on displaying property information without requiring full marketing materials from agents. This comes during a period of significant change for the platform, following the departure of high-profile advisory board member Verona Frankish after less than 24 hours in the role.

The company emphasised its commitment to transparency, stating: "To our knowledge, no agent has ever paid us anything for an applicant enquiry. If it has happened, it was in error and we would gladly provide a refund." However, the explanation didn't specifically address why the test viewing request triggered a payment prompt.

As the property market continues to evolve with digital solutions, homeowners and industry professionals alike may wish to monitor how emerging platforms balance innovative approaches with traditional service expectations. The developments at BestAgent highlight ongoing discussions about sustainable business models in online property services.

The proposed charges would vary according to property price points, which the company argues could give agents more control over marketing expenditure compared to traditional portal subscription models.

BestAgent's statement also addressed concerns about its approach to property listings, reaffirming its position on displaying property information without requiring full marketing materials from agents. This comes during a period of significant change for the platform, following the departure of high-profile advisory board member Verona Frankish after less than 24 hours in the role.

The company emphasised its commitment to transparency, stating: "To our knowledge, no agent has ever paid us anything for an applicant enquiry. As the property market continues to evolve with digital solutions, homeowners and industry professionals alike may wish to monitor how emerging platforms balance innovative approaches with traditional service expectations. item.title: Property auction sales slump as market suffers sharp slowdown
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The UK property auction market experienced a notable dip in October, with residential sales volumes falling by 14.6% compared to the same period last year. Industry data reveals the total value raised across all property auctions declined by 11.2% to £543.3 million, while the number of lots offered dropped by 8.2% annually. The national success rate also softened to 65.3%, down from 68.3% in October 2025.

Mixed Performance Across Sectors and Regions

Whilst residential auctions struggled, commercial property sales bucked the trend with a 5.7% increase in transactions and a striking 66% surge in total proceeds. Regional performance varied significantly, with London, East Anglia and Scotland recording growth in both lots offered and sold during the rolling quarter. Yorkshire and The Humber also saw a healthy 24.3% rise in the value raised at auction.

However, other areas faced challenges. The South-East Home Counties and North-West regions reported declines in both sales volumes and total proceeds. This regional variation suggests local market conditions continue to influence auction performance across the country.

Calendar Shifts and Longer-Term Trends

Industry experts note that changes to auction schedules may have contributed to October's weaker figures, with some sales shifting into September or November. David Sandeman of EIG commented: "Monthly comparisons can be affected by the timing of individual sales. With several auctions moving into November, the coming weeks should provide a clearer picture."

Despite the monthly dip, the twelve-month rolling figures present a more positive outlook. Both lots offered and sold continue to exceed year-earlier levels, with residential auctions showing a 10% increase in lots offered and a 7.8% rise in sales over this longer timeframe. The total value raised across all property types in the twelve months to October stood at £5.96 billion, up 4.5% year-on-year.

As the property market enters the final weeks of the year, potential buyers and sellers may wish to monitor auction activity closely. The traditional seasonal slowdown, combined with shifting auction calendars, could present both challenges and opportunities for those considering this route to property transactions.

item.title: Property transactions set to fall in 2026 before rebounding next year
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

UK property transactions could see a dip in 2026 before rebounding the following year, according to fresh analysis from estate agency group eXp UK. The research suggests a 4.4% annual decline in residential sales across Britain this year, with Scotland potentially facing a more prolonged downturn compared to other nations.

Mixed fortunes across UK regions

The forecast indicates approximately 1.16 million property transactions in 2026, down from 1.21 million in 2025. However, the market could see a 6.7% recovery in 2027, potentially pushing sales volumes to around 1.24 million.

England appears set to lead this recovery, with projections showing a 7.9% increase in transactions during 2027 following an expected 4.6% decline this year. Wales and Northern Ireland may experience more modest fluctuations, with both nations forecast to see small decreases in 2026 before returning to growth in 2027.

Scotland presents a different picture, with analysts predicting consecutive annual declines of 5.2% in 2026 and 2.3% in 2027. If accurate, this would take annual transactions below 100,000 for the first time in recent years.

Economic factors influencing the market

Adam Day, head of eXp UK and Europe, noted: "The property market has faced significant challenges recently, and our projections suggest 2026 may see transaction volumes finish below last year's levels. The 2027 outlook appears more positive, with England particularly well-placed to drive recovery."

Several key factors could influence whether these projections materialise:

  • Mortgage affordability and interest rate trends
  • Broader economic conditions and employment levels
  • First-time buyer support schemes and government policies
  • Regional variations in housing supply and demand

The analysis used HMRC transaction data with an exponential smoothing model to create these projections. While such forecasting methods provide useful indicators, Day cautioned that "the strength of any recovery will ultimately depend on wider economic conditions and buyer confidence".

For homeowners considering a move, these projections may help inform timing decisions, though local market conditions can vary significantly from national trends. Those monitoring the market might wish to keep an eye on mortgage rate movements and regional price indicators when planning their next steps.

item.title: Rental listings hit seven-year high as supply outstrips tenant demand
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Asturi

The UK rental market is experiencing a significant shift, with new property listings reaching a seven-year high whilst tenant demand grows at a markedly slower pace. According to recent data from TwentyEA, rental supply has increased by 10.4% so far in 2026 – representing 118,100 more available properties compared to the same period last year. Meanwhile, demand measured by lets agreed has risen by just 2.7%, creating a widening gap that could offer tenants greater choice in certain areas.

Regional variations in rental market trends

Analysis reveals striking regional differences across the UK rental landscape. Wales has emerged as the standout performer, with a 22.1% annual increase in rental listings alongside an 11.3% rise in lets agreed – the strongest demand growth nationwide. Most regions followed similar patterns, with 12 out of 13 areas showing increased supply and nine experiencing growth exceeding 10%.

Inner London presents a contrasting picture, where a 6.3% rise in available properties coincides with a 1.1% decline in lets agreed. This divergence highlights how local market conditions can vary considerably, with some regions seeing landlords benefit from strong tenant interest whilst others face softening demand.

Price bracket performance and rental values

The increase in rental supply spans all price points, with mid-range properties (£800-£1,500 pcm) showing the most notable growth at 12.6%. More affordable homes (below £800 pcm) saw an 11.2% uplift, suggesting landlords across market segments are bringing properties to let.

Despite the supply surge, average UK rents have remained relatively stable, increasing just £13 (0.9%) to £1,493 per month. Regional variations exist though – the North West recorded one of the highest rises at 4.4% (£48), whilst Wales and the North East saw no change in average rents. Interestingly, the £1,500-£3,000 bracket experienced a 0.9% decline in lets agreed, possibly indicating changing tenant preferences or affordability pressures.

Understanding the market dynamics

While increased listings might suggest improving conditions for tenants, industry experts caution that the figures could mask underlying challenges. Landlords continue to exit the private rented sector at a rate of 562 properties daily, raising questions about whether the supply growth represents genuine new availability or simply existing properties being remarketed.

Prospective renters might find the current conditions present opportunities to negotiate terms, particularly in areas where supply growth significantly outstrips demand. However, with regional variations so pronounced, local market research remains essential for both landlords and tenants navigating this evolving landscape.

item.title: Tenants rethink what they’ll pay extra for as rental priorities shift
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

New research reveals a significant shift in what UK tenants prioritise when renting properties, with high-speed broadband, energy efficiency and transport links now topping the list of must-haves. Meanwhile, demand for some traditional communal facilities appears to be waning as renters reassess what they're willing to pay extra for.

Shifting priorities for modern tenants

A comprehensive survey of over 450 renters by property consultancy Carter Jonas shows that nearly 90% of tenants now consider reliable broadband essential, while 82% prioritise energy-efficient homes. Other key factors include:

  • Access to public transport (valued by 80% of respondents)
  • Private outdoor space (important for 70%)
  • Dedicated home office areas (a priority for 57%)

The findings suggest that landlords might benefit more from investing in a property's fundamental features rather than expensive add-ons. Interestingly, the research shows growing interest in certain lifestyle amenities, with 47% of tenants willing to pay extra for on-site gym access - a significant increase from 29% just two years ago.

What tenants will - and won't - pay extra for

The study highlights changing attitudes towards premium facilities. While outdoor spaces and fitness options are gaining popularity, demand has dropped sharply for:

  • On-site management teams (down from 44% to 31%)
  • Shared indoor facilities like workspaces and libraries (falling from 44% to 25%)

Experts suggest this shift indicates tenants increasingly view many services as standard expectations rather than premium extras worth additional payment. Property professionals note that landlords who regularly review tenant preferences may be better placed to make strategic investment decisions about their rentals.

Affordability remains the primary concern for most renters, with nearly 30% citing it as their top priority when considering future rental homes. Energy efficiency and property maintenance also featured prominently in tenant responses, highlighting the ongoing importance of practical considerations alongside lifestyle preferences.

For those navigating the rental market, these insights may help inform decisions about what features to prioritise when searching for a new home. As tenant expectations continue to evolve, both renters and landlords may need to adapt to these changing priorities in the years ahead.

item.title: Landlord Law Newsround #463
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK property market continues to evolve rapidly, with significant developments affecting both landlords and tenants. From energy efficiency challenges to licensing fines and possession cases, landlords face an increasingly complex regulatory landscape. This week’s update examines key trends that could impact buy-to-let investors across England and Wales.

EPC Upgrades Present Challenges for Landlords

New research highlights rising concerns among landlords about meeting upcoming energy efficiency targets. With all rental properties required to achieve at least an EPC ‘C’ rating by 2030, many face practical hurdles in implementing necessary upgrades. Industry experts point to several key issues:

  • Tenant awareness about EPC ratings remains surprisingly low
  • Concerns persist that upgrade costs may lead to rent increases
  • Landlords report confusion about available support schemes
  • Some question the reliability of EPC assessments themselves

The findings have prompted renewed calls for government-backed financing options to help landlords fund energy efficiency improvements without passing costs onto tenants.

London Licensing Fines Reach Record Levels

Recent analysis reveals London landlords have paid over £16.9 million in licensing fines, with penalties averaging £5,000 per offence. Licensing breaches now account for nearly 60% of all property-related fines recorded in the capital. Key findings include:

  • Civil penalties make up £15.4 million of total fines
  • The average licence costs just £764 compared to typical fines
  • 29 of London’s 32 boroughs now operate additional licensing schemes

With councils able to issue penalties up to £40,000 without court proceedings, property owners are advised to regularly check local licensing requirements. Experts recommend verifying whether properties need licences before renting them out, and conducting checks every six months as schemes frequently change.

New Guidance on Possession Cases

Recent legal cases have clarified how landlords can use Ground 1A under the Renters’ Reform Act to regain possession when selling properties. Courts now require clear evidence of a genuine intention to sell, including:

  • Documented plans to market the property
  • Communication with estate agents
  • Proof that selling with vacant possession offers better value

In one notable case, a landlord acting as executor successfully regained possession after providing evidence of their settled intention to sell, even without having identified a specific buyer. This sets an important precedent for similar cases moving forward.

These developments highlight the importance of staying informed about regulatory changes in the private rental sector. Landlords may wish to seek professional advice to navigate these evolving requirements effectively.

item.title: Tributes paid to well-respected estate agent after almost 40 years in the industry
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The UK property industry is mourning the loss of Stuart Cole, a highly respected estate agent who passed away after a courageous battle with cancer. With nearly 40 years’ experience in the sector, Cole built an exceptional reputation in the prestigious country house markets of Surrey and Berkshire, leaving behind a legacy of professional excellence and personal warmth.

A distinguished career in prime property

Beginning his estate agency journey in 1988, Cole developed particular expertise in North Surrey and Berkshire’s exclusive residential markets. His deep knowledge of prestigious private estates like Wentworth and St George’s Hill made him a sought-after advisor for high-net-worth clients. After establishing himself in Cornwall’s property market, he joined global agency Knight Frank in 2014, where he continued to cultivate an international network of buyers and sellers.

Colleagues describe Cole as having an unparalleled understanding of the country house market, with an ability to match discerning clients with exceptional properties. Throughout his career, he facilitated transactions involving some of the South East’s most desirable homes, earning recognition as one of the sector’s most accomplished professionals.

Remembered for his vibrant personality

While Cole’s professional achievements were substantial, those who knew him emphasise that his character made the deepest impression. James Cleland, head of country sales at Knight Frank, remembers his colleague as "a larger-than-life personality who approached everything with energy, humour and determination".

Despite his serious cancer diagnosis, Cole maintained his trademark positivity and dedication to clients, never allowing his illness to overshadow his professional commitment or zest for life. An enthusiastic golfer, skier and five-a-side football player, he balanced his demanding career with active pursuits and cherished time with family in Cornwall, where he enjoyed coastal walks with his dog.

The property community has lost not just a skilled professional, but a man who transformed client relationships into genuine friendships. His passing leaves a void in the country house market where his expertise and vibrant presence were widely valued.

Knight Frank has established channels for colleagues, clients and friends to send condolences to Cole’s family, with James Cleland coordinating messages either by post to their Baker Street office or via email. The response reflects the profound respect and affection earned by an estate agent who embodied both professional excellence and personal warmth throughout his four-decade career.

item.title: Is the UK property market ‘closed until further notice’?
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Despite gloomy headlines suggesting the UK property market has ground to a halt, recent data shows buyers are still actively agreeing sales across the country. However, estate agents continue to face significant challenges in this complex landscape, where market conditions often mask deeper operational issues within the industry itself.

Market Activity Defies the Doom-Mongers

The narrative of a frozen property market doesn't match the reality of ongoing transactions, though estate agents know all too well how fragile these deals can be. The collapse of a property chain after weeks of careful negotiation remains a painful experience for all parties involved, particularly when livelihoods depend on successful completions.

Valuation practices have emerged as a particular pressure point, with some agents reporting losing listings after competitors promised unrealistic prices. This creates difficult conversations weeks later when properties fail to sell at inflated valuations. While tempting in the short term, such tactics ultimately damage trust in the profession.

Agents Face Tough Choices in Challenging Conditions

Industry experts suggest many challenges stem from controllable factors rather than market conditions alone. Common issues include prematurely reduced fees without client prompting, or failing to proactively adjust pricing strategies when viewings dry up. The recent Budget and global economic uncertainty have undoubtedly given buyers pause, but these factors don't explain all the sector's current difficulties.

Property professionals might consider reviewing their approach to:

  • Maintaining honest valuation practices even when competitors overpromise
  • Proactively communicating with vendors about necessary price adjustments
  • Focusing on completing sales rather than just winning instructions

Taking Control in an Uncertain Market

For agents experiencing a difficult period, industry leaders recommend practical steps like reviewing current stock and identifying which vendors might benefit from a proactive call about pricing or marketing strategy. As highlighted in recent industry discussions, the difference between struggling and thriving often comes down to execution rather than market conditions.

While the property market undoubtedly presents challenges, the data shows opportunities remain for those willing to adapt. Both buyers and sellers continue to transact, and agents who focus on delivering results rather than excuses may find they can navigate this complex period more successfully.

item.title: Leasehold shake-up sparks warnings over property sales, costs and legal chaos
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The government's proposed leasehold reforms have drawn mixed reactions from property experts, with industry voices warning of potential disruption to sales, increased costs and unforeseen complications for homeowners. While broadly supporting the move towards commonhold ownership, professionals caution that the transition requires careful implementation to avoid repeating past legislative missteps.

Industry calls for measured approach to leasehold reforms

Property professionals have welcomed the intention behind the Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill, which aims to make commonhold the default ownership model for new flats in England and Wales. However, concerns have emerged about the practical challenges of implementation. The Conveyancing Task Force has highlighted risks of rushed legislation, drawing parallels with the problematic rollout of the Building Safety Act.

Key industry figures argue that political priorities shouldn't overshadow technical considerations. They're urging ministers to consult conveyancers, mortgage lenders and property lawyers before finalising the legislation. Several crucial details about valuation methods and implementation timelines remain unclear, with much dependent on secondary legislation yet to be published.

The reforms propose significant changes including:

  • A £250 annual cap on ground rents
  • Simplified lease extension processes
  • Easier conversion from leasehold to commonhold

item.title: Comings & Goings
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Northern Ireland's property market sees movement this month as John Minnis Estate Agents announces a key leadership appointment alongside expansion plans, while an experienced agent joins a national consultancy firm.

John Minnis Estate Agents Expands Leadership Team

Northern Ireland's John Minnis Estate Agents has strengthened its leadership with the appointment of Lynzi Templeton as director. The move comes as the firm prepares for its next phase of growth, including a planned sixth branch opening in south Belfast by 2027.

Templeton brings over two decades of estate agency and operational experience to the role. The company currently operates five branches across Belfast, Holywood, Bangor, Comber and Donaghadee, with the south Belfast expansion set to complete its network across the region.

Founder John Minnis commented: "Lynzi's operational expertise comes at a pivotal moment as we prepare for expansion. With our strong leadership team in place, we're well positioned for this next chapter of growth."

Industry Veteran Joins Estate Agent Coaching Firm

Meanwhile, Hayley Chambers, founder of Chambers Estates, has joined The Estate Agent Consultancy (TEAC) as a business coach. Chambers will draw on her seven years' experience in residential sales, lettings and valuations to mentor both employed and self-employed agents.

Having built her own agency from scratch, Chambers specialises in the challenges facing independent operators. Her coaching will focus on business development, client acquisition and balancing professional demands with personal commitments.

"Running your own agency requires completely different skills to being an employed agent," Chambers noted. "Having navigated those challenges myself, I understand exactly what independent operators need to thrive."

TEAC founder Chris Webb added: "Hayley's first-hand experience of building a successful independent agency makes her invaluable to our coaching team."

These appointments highlight the ongoing evolution within the UK property sector, with established firms strengthening their leadership while experienced professionals share their expertise through consultancy roles. For homeowners in Northern Ireland, the expansion of John Minnis Estate Agents may provide additional local options when buying or selling property in the coming years.

item.title: How Does Property Compare with Other Assets in an Uncertain Market?
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

During periods of economic volatility, investors and homeowners often reassess their asset allocation strategies. UK residential property has long been considered a relatively stable investment compared to more volatile markets, but how does bricks-and-mortar measure up against alternatives like equities, commodities and fixed-income securities when uncertainty looms?

Property Versus Traditional Asset Classes

Property investment offers several distinctive characteristics during turbulent times. Unlike stocks which can swing dramatically within hours, residential property values tend to move more gradually, providing a cushion against sudden market shocks. The UK's chronic housing shortage also provides fundamental support to prices, though liquidity is considerably lower than with securities.

When comparing property to gold - the classic 'safe haven' asset - the differences are pronounced. Gold provides instant liquidity and acts as a hedge against inflation, but generates no income. Residential property offers rental yields alongside capital growth potential, though requires active management. Bonds typically deliver steadier returns than property but currently struggle to outpace inflation, while equities may offer higher growth potential but with greater volatility.

Key Considerations for Property Investors

For those considering property investment during uncertain periods, several factors warrant careful attention:

  • Location resilience: Certain UK regions and property types have historically shown more stability during downturns
  • Rental demand: Areas with strong employment markets tend to maintain better occupancy rates
  • Financing costs: Mortgage rates significantly impact investment returns, making product selection crucial
  • Tax efficiency: Recent changes to landlord taxation have altered the maths for some investors

Property's tangible nature often appeals to investors wary of more abstract financial instruments during unstable periods. The ability to add value through refurbishment or development can also provide returns not available with purely financial assets.

Whilst past performance never guarantees future results, UK residential property has demonstrated considerable resilience through various economic cycles, though typically with less dramatic highs and lows than more liquid markets. Investors might consider how property could complement other assets in their portfolio rather than viewing it as an either/or proposition.

item.title: House price growth stalls as estate agents warn of further falls
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The UK housing market has shown signs of stagnation, with annual house price growth remaining at 1.2% as of September 2023, according to the latest data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS). Average house prices in the UK now stand at £273,000, reflecting a subdued market influenced by higher mortgage costs, reduced buyer confidence, and ongoing affordability challenges. Whilst this figure represents modest growth, the national average conceals significant regional variations, with some areas experiencing sharper declines while others continue to see price increases.

Regional Variations in House Price Trends

The ONS figures highlight stark differences in property price movements across the UK. In England, house prices rose by just 0.8% annually, while Wales and Scotland saw stronger growth at 1.8% and 2.3% respectively. London remains the weakest performer, with prices falling by 3.5% over the year. Inner London recorded an even steeper decline of 7.2%, marking its most significant annual drop since August 2009. In contrast, the North East of England emerged as the strongest regional market, with prices climbing by 4.6% over the same period.

These regional disparities underscore the uneven impact of economic pressures on the property market. Factors such as local affordability, demand, and employment opportunities continue to shape trends, creating a patchwork of growth and decline across the country.

Shifting Dynamics for Buyers and Sellers

Estate agents report that the current market conditions are prompting changes in buyer behaviour. With higher mortgage costs and weaker consumer confidence, buyers are taking longer to make decisions and are increasingly selective about their purchases. This shift has given buyers greater negotiating power, particularly in areas where properties are overpriced or where demand is softer.

Nicky Stevenson, managing director of Fine & Country, emphasised the importance of realistic pricing for sellers. “Buyers now have more choice than they’ve had in years, meaning overpriced properties are increasingly likely to be overlooked. The difference between setting the right asking price from the outset and having to reduce it later can be significant.” Similarly, Verona Frankish, CEO of Yopa, noted that the challenge for sellers lies not just in achieving a strong price but in finding the right buyer in a more cautious market.

Daniel Clarke, founder of Homebuyer.Agency, added that whilst buyers have more room to negotiate, they should not assume they can dictate prices entirely. “A more measured market doesn’t mean buyers can simply name their price. Realistic offers and careful negotiation remain key.”

Rising Rents and Market Outlook

As the property market slows, rental demand continues to grow, pushing UK private rents up by 3.8% in the year to October 2023. The average monthly rent now stands at £1,411, adding further pressure on tenants and highlighting the broader affordability challenges facing the housing market.

Looking ahead, industry experts suggest that house prices could face further downward pressure if mortgage costs remain high and economic uncertainty persists. Whilst the market has shown resilience in some areas, the combination of affordability constraints and cautious buyer behaviour may continue to weigh on growth in the coming months.

For homeowners and prospective buyers, staying informed about local market trends and seeking professional advice could prove invaluable in navigating these challenging conditions.

item.title: Rental demand takes unexpected dip as sales market holds steady
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Recent data from Propertymark has revealed an unexpected dip in tenant registrations across the UK rental market, raising questions about shifting demand dynamics. Whilst the sales market has remained relatively stable, the lettings sector appears to be experiencing a slowdown, even as rental costs continue to rise. This development comes amidst ongoing economic uncertainty, prompting both tenants and landlords to reassess their positions.

Rental Market Faces Unusual Slowdown

According to Propertymark’s latest Housing Insight Report, letting agents reported fewer tenant registrations in September compared to previous months. This decline marks a potential departure from recent trends, though it remains unclear whether this signals a long-term shift in demand. Despite rental inflation easing in recent months, overall monthly costs continue to climb, adding pressure to tenants already grappling with affordability challenges.

Nathan Emerson, Chief Executive of Propertymark, commented on the findings, stating, “Whilst rental inflation has slowed, monthly costs are still rising, underscoring the ongoing pressures faced by tenants.” This suggests that affordability issues may be influencing tenant activity, with many households prioritising essential expenses over moving or securing new rental agreements.

Sales Market Shows Resilience

In contrast to the rental sector, the UK sales market has demonstrated greater stability. Propertymark’s report highlights that transaction volumes have remained steady compared to the previous year, with gross mortgage advances showing little significant movement. This indicates that buyers and sellers are continuing to transact despite higher borrowing costs and broader economic uncertainties.

Emerson noted, “The number of property transactions has remained consistent with last year’s figures, and gross mortgage advances have also stayed relatively stable.” However, mortgage affordability and household finances remain key factors influencing purchasing decisions, with many potential buyers carefully weighing their options before committing to a property purchase.

Landlord Investment Under Pressure

The report also sheds light on the challenges facing landlords and property investors. Economic uncertainty, coupled with rising financing costs, has made portfolio expansion increasingly difficult. Many landlords are reassessing their investments in light of these pressures, with some opting to hold off on further acquisitions or even reduce their existing portfolios.

This cautious approach could have implications for the rental market’s future supply, potentially exacerbating affordability issues for tenants if fewer properties become available. For those considering entering the buy-to-let market, it could be worth carefully evaluating current conditions and seeking professional advice to navigate the complexities of property investment in the current climate.

As the UK property market continues to evolve, homeowners, tenants, and investors alike may wish to stay informed about these trends. Whilst the sales market remains steady, the rental sector’s unexpected dip highlights the importance of monitoring affordability and demand dynamics in the months ahead.
